output:
S: Patient reports painless blurry vision in the right eye for one week. Reports intermittent fevers, headache, body aches, and a nonpruritic maculopapular rash on lower legs for the past 6 months. Denies neck stiffness, nausea, vomiting, Raynaud's phenomenon, oral ulcerations, chest pain, shortness of breath, abdominal pain, photosensitivity, and toxic habits. Reports an isolated episode of left knee swelling and testicular swelling in the past.

O: Vital signs were normal. Physical exam revealed bilateral papilledema and optic nerve erythema in the right eye (greater than the left). Right inferior nasal quadrant visual field defect and a right afferent pupillary defect were noted. Muscle strength and reflexes were normal, and sensation was intact. Maculopapular rash was noted on bilateral lower extremities. Admitting labs showed microcytic anemia (Hemoglobin 11.6 gm/dL, Hematocrit 35.3%, MCV 76.9 fL), hyponatremia (Sodium 133 mmol/L), elevated Erythrocyte Sedimentation Rate (ESR) of 33 mm/hr, and elevated C-reactive protein (CRP) of 13.3 mg/L. Urinalysis showed no protein or blood. Lumbar puncture fluid was clear and colorless, with 2 red blood cells per microliter and 56 white blood cells per microliter.

A: Preliminary assessment indicates an underlying inflammatory or infectious process.

P: Additional tests will be run, and a specialist will be consulted to determine the cause of symptoms. Supportive care will be provided in the meantime, and the patient will be kept informed about new findings and treatment options.

S: Patient is a 7-year-old boy with congenital bilateral sensorineural deafness and a history of a failed right cochlear implant.
O: MRI was performed with the airway secured using a size 5.5 mm internal-diameter uncuffed ETT. Intraoperative monitoring included brainstem auditory sensory evoked potentials, brainstem mapping of CN IX, X, XI, XII motor nuclei, and corticobulbar tract motor-evoked potential (MEP). Laryngeal electrode used was 32 mm by 29 mm for CN X monitoring. Measurements taken were 6 cm at vocal cords (15 cm at lips). Total Intravenous Anesthesia (TIVA) was administered using propofol (target plasma concentration 3.5–5.0 mcg/ml) and remifentanil (0.08–0.3 mcg/kg/min).
A: Preliminary assessment based on surgical preparation and monitoring for ABI insertion.
P: Intraoperative neurophysiology monitoring was performed, including brainstem auditory sensory evoked potentials, brainstem mapping of CN IX, X, XI, XII motor nuclei, and corticobulbar tract MEP. The anesthesia team managed lead placement for CN IX, X, XI, XII using the specified electrodes. Post-surgery recovery will be closely monitored.

S: Patient reports history of thyroid nodule identified via ultrasound in April 2017. Postoperative course following total thyroidectomy and central neck dissection was uneventful, with transient hypocalcemia on the first day which resolved within 48 hours.
O: Ultrasound (April 2017): Single thyroid nodule in the left lobe, largest diameter 1 cm. Biochemical screening results: Calcitonin level 40 ng/mL (Normal range 1-4.8 ng/mL). Stimulation test with intravenous calcium resulted in calcitonin levels peaking at 1420 ng/mL. Histopathology of removed tissue revealed medullary thyroid cancer (MTC), 1 cm. Tumor cells were positive for calcitonin, Cromogranin A, Synaptofisin, and TTF-1, but negative for amyloid. Focal foci of C-cells hyperplasia were present throughout the gland. No signs of metastasis in central lymph nodes.
A: Medullary thyroid cancer confirmed by immunohistochemistry. Postoperative course was uneventful with transient hypocalcemia resolving spontaneously.
P: Total thyroidectomy and central neck dissection performed due to elevated calcitonin levels following stimulation testing. Patient discharged after recovery. Continue with regular follow-up appointments and monitoring for condition management.

S: Patient reports a one-week history of progressive headache, nausea, and vomiting. Patient also noticed right-side weakness, ptosis, and diplopia. Patient reported an acute onset conscious disturbance with Glasgow Coma Scale of E3VaM5 at the hospital.
O: Brain computed tomography revealed an enhanced brain tumor with necrotic cystic changes located in the left temporal lobe with upward extension to the left basal ganglion and periventricular region, causing perifocal edema and midline shift. Prior pathology included classic GBM (pleomorphic, hyperchromatic cells, glassy astrocytic cytoplasm, hypercellularity, microvascular proliferation, necrosis). Follow-up MRI (June 2014) revealed a new enhanced nodular lesion, 1.1 cm in diameter, at the left temporal base. Follow-up MRI (October 2014) showed progressive change in lesions, with a maximum of 3.0 cm in diameter. Pathology from gross tumor removal showed an oligodendroglial component, IDH1 positivity, p53 positivity, and MGMT negativity. Third debulking surgery pathology revealed both GBM- and PNET-like components; the PNET-like component exhibited positivity for synaptophysin and CD56 and focal weak positivity for glial fibrillary.
A: History of multiple brain tumors, including classic GBM, with subsequent surgical resection and radiotherapy/chemotherapy. Follow-up imaging revealed progressive changes and new lesions. Increased intracranial pressure was noted in May 2015, necessitating a third debulking surgery.
P: Continue to monitor condition closely and provide further treatment options as needed. Patient instructed to follow up regularly.

S: Patient reports development of severe abdominal pain. History includes hepatocellular carcinoma and a liver transplantation from a living donor approximately one year ago. Patient reported experiencing nausea/vomiting, elevated blood pressure, and restlessness 12 hours after discontinuation of continuous intravenous fentanyl infusion. Pancreatitis with abdominal pain recurred transiently one month later.
O: Continuous intravenous fentanyl was administered at 1200 μg/day, increased to 2400 μg/day (MED 240 mg/day), and then reduced to 240 μg/day before discontinuation. Pancreatic enzyme inhibitor, antibiotic, and fluid were administered. Transdermal fentanyl patch was initiated. IV fentanyl infusion was resumed at 240 μg/day, then titrated to 600 μg/day, followed by a gradual daily decrease (600, 300, 240, 180, 120, and 60 μg/day). Fentanyl was discontinued 64 days after the onset of withdrawal symptoms.
A: Management of acute pancreatitis and abdominal pain with opioid titration and supportive care. Successful management of fentanyl withdrawal.
P: Continuous intravenous fentanyl infusion was resumed at 240 μg/day, then titrated to 600 μg/day. Fentanyl was gradually decreased daily (600, 300, 240, 180, 120, and 60 μg/day). Fentanyl was discontinued without causing withdrawal symptoms 64 days after onset of withdrawal symptoms. Patient instructed to continue monitoring symptoms and report any discomfort or changes in condition.

S: Patient reports pain in the right chest. Patient denies smoking history and asbestos exposure. Patient reports decreased forced vital capacity (FVC) over the previous 3 years and developed shortness of breath on exertion, leading to restrictive respiratory failure.

O: Physical examination revealed a reduction of lung sounds at the right lung basis, but no clinical sign of autoimmune disease. Chest X-ray showed a considerable reduction in the right lung volume with associated right pleural effusion. CT scan revealed a slight reduction in right lung volume with associated right pleural effusion and pleural thickening. Serological, autoimmune, and microbiological tests were negative. PET-CT showed low-intensity hyper-accumulation of 18-FDG in the right pleura with increased concentration in the basal, middle, and posterior pleural surface. Surgical lung biopsy identified non-specific fibrinous pleurisy; search for neoplastic or infectious cells was negative.

A: Right pleural effusion and pleural thickening noted on imaging. Findings are consistent with non-specific fibrinous pleurisy.

P: Prednisolone course prescribed to help with symptoms. Further investigations included chest X-ray, computed tomography (CT) scan, serological, autoimmune, and microbiological tests, echocardiography, phrenic nerve stimulation test, and total body PET-CT. Surgical lung biopsy was performed.

S: Patient presented with body weight loss. Reports history of hypertension and diabetes, both well-controlled by medication.
O: Hemoglobin 9.1 g/dl. Tumor markers within normal limits. Colonoscopy revealed a circumferential tumor in the sigmoid colon. Histological examination showed RAS-mutant adenocarcinoma. Contrast-enhanced CT scan showed irregular colonic wall thickening with massive involvement of the urinary bladder and enlarged regional lymph nodes suggestive of metastases but no distant metastasis. Pretreatment diagnosis LACC stage IIIC (T4bN2M0). Postoperative findings: Sigmoid colectomy and partial resection of the bladder were performed without neurogenic voiding dysfunction or urinary incontinence. Pathological examination revealed tumor cells or degeneration in less than one third of the entire lesion, consistent with grade 1a effect according to the Japanese Classification of Colorectal Carcinoma. Final pathological diagnosis: ypT4b, ypN0, M0, ypStage IIC.
A: RAS-mutant adenocarcinoma of the sigmoid colon, ypStage IIC (ypT4b, ypN0, M0).
P: Treatment included a loop transverse colostomy followed by 5 courses of CAPOX plus bevacizumab and 1 course without oxaliplatin due to grade 2 neurotoxicity. Subsequent surgery involved sigmoid colectomy and partial bladder resection. Adjuvant chemotherapy consisted of 8 courses of capecitabine alone. No recurrence at 16 months post-diagnosis. Continue monitoring progress.

S: Patient reports a 6-month history of swelling in the left floor of the mouth and difficulty in swallowing. Denies pain or tongue paralysis.
O: Intraoral examination revealed a well-defined 3.5 × 3 × 2 cm solid, spherical submucosal nodule adjacent to the sublingual gland covered with light bluish smooth mucus. Patient reported slight pain upon pressure application. Tongue mobility and sensory functions were normal. No lymphadenopathy was detected in the submandibular region on palpation. Laboratory results were normal. Enhanced computed tomography scan revealed a 2.8 × 1.8 × 2.1 cm well-defined, solid, heterogeneous nodule occupying the left floor of the mouth with abundant blood flow. No enlarged lymph nodes were detected in the submental or submandibular regions.
A: Initial clinical impression is that this could be a benign salivary gland tumor, dermoid cyst, or benign connective tissue neoplasm.
P: Schedule for surgery via an intraoral approach to remove the tumor and further examine it. Post-surgery plan includes fixing the tissue sample with 10% formalin for histopathological diagnosis.

S: Patient reports tingling and numbness in the right arm and leg for at least one month. Patient has a history of prostate cancer and underwent a prostatectomy. Patient reports unsteady gait and needed assistance when moving. Denies smoking, alcohol use, or drug use.

O: Vital signs upon admission were Temperature 97.9 F, Heart Rate 68 beats/min, Blood Pressure 137/84 mmHg, and Respiratory Rate 18 breaths per minute. Neurological examination revealed right-sided hemiparesis; right arm strength was 4/5, and right leg strength was 3/5. Left side was unremarkable. Cranial nerves 2-10 were normal. Patient had difficulty shrugging the right shoulder and could not turn the head to the left. Gait was unsteady, compensating with the non-affected side. Laboratory values were within normal limits. Head CT and follow-up MRI were negative for a stroke. Cervical spine CT showed marked degenerative changes, including moderate to severe spinal canal stenosis at C4/C5. Cervical spine MRI confirmed moderate to severe central stenosis with cord compression and mildly increased T2 signal at C4/C5 and C5/C6, along with degenerative findings between levels C3-C7 and hypertrophy.

A: Preliminary assessment of right-sided neurological symptoms and cervical spinal stenosis.

P: Follow up with primary care physician and a specialist to address the spinal stenosis and related symptoms. Discuss potential treatment options and closely monitor condition.

S: 76-year-old woman presenting with backache for 4 days without obvious cause. History of hypertension and lumbar spinal canal stenosis. Symptoms aggravated suddenly with vomiting and difficulty with body movement. Patient reports no prior treatment with oral anticoagulant or antiplatelet agents.
O: Body temperature 36.2°C, blood pressure 192/109 mmHg, pulse 79/min. Glasgow Coma Scale (GCS) E4, V4, M6. Lumbar spinal MRI (4 days post-onset) showed a band-like shadow continuous from the thoracic spinal level with high intensity on T1-weighted imaging and low intensity on T2-weighted imaging and STIR. Thoracic spinal MRI (7 days post-onset) revealed a band-like shadow extending from Th2 to L3 on the subdural extramedullary ventral side, and a mass present at Th7 compressing and deforming the spinal cord centered on this region with changes in intramedullary brightness of Th6. Neurological examination showed no hypesthesia or muscle weakness of the lower limbs. Deep tendon reflexes were normal. Hemorrhage and coagulation test findings were normal. Plain radiography at admission showed no abnormal findings in the thoracolumbar vertebrae.
A: Preliminary assessment indicates a mass compressing the spinal cord which may be causing the backache and other symptoms.
P: Further tests will be performed, and potential treatment options will be discussed with the patient.

S: Patient reports a history of seizures and abnormal neurological findings. Diagnosed with HHH syndrome at age 4. Reports issues with expressive language and attention problems, confirmed by a neuropsychiatric evaluation. Reports significant myopia. Childhood diet included protein restriction to 1.5 g/kg/d for HHH syndrome management. Weight has been at the 25th percentile and height less than the 3rd percentile throughout life. History of three children. First pregnancy involved nausea and dizziness; low-protein diet in the first trimester. Mild hyperammonemia was detected during the 11th and 12th week of pregnancy, requiring protein restriction to 40 g/d. Developed seizures at 22 weeks gestation and was started on carbamazepine. Brain imaging showed multiple small calcifications of unreported cause, but normal cerebral angiography. First child was delivered via Cesarean section with intrauterine growth restriction (weight less than the 3rd percentile); development was normal at 2 years of age. Second child's cord blood showed moderately elevated ornithine concentration (302 μM/L), which decreased to normal in newborn blood 24 hours post-birth. Ammonia levels increased 24 hours postpartum after the birth of the second child, requiring treatment with oral sodium benzoate and intravenous arginine. Third child experienced transient respiratory distress at birth. Second child had normal growth and development at 10 months of age.

O: No specific objective measurements were provided in the dialogue.

A: History of HHH syndrome, associated neurological issues, and complex obstetric history including hyperammonemia during pregnancy and neonatal complications.

P: Continue to monitor condition and children's development closely. Patient instructed to maintain prescribed diet and medication regimen.

S: Patient is a 36-year-old G2P1 Caucasian woman currently 9 weeks pregnant. Reports recent headaches. Denies visual changes, chest pain, dyspnea, or other neurological symptoms. History includes previous IVF pregnancy complicated by preeclampsia at 27 weeks and delivery of a growth-restricted fetus (1900 g) by C-section at 36 weeks. Past history of infrarenal aortic stenosis (75% stenosis with hypertrophied internal mammary and epigastric arteries). Regular medications include aspirin 100 mg and calcium 1.2 g daily. Family history significant for paternal ischemic heart disease and maternal hypertension.

O: Laboratory investigations for preeclampsia showed low-grade proteinuria with a urine protein/creatinine ratio of 40 mg/mmol, normal renal and liver function. Vasculitic screen results were C-reactive protein (CRP) 3.8 mg/L, erythrocyte sedimentation rate (ESR) 16 mm/h, and absence of antinuclear antibodies, antineutrophilic cytoplasmic antibodies, anti-double-stranded DNA antibodies, and antiphospholipid antibodies. Ultrasound at 34 weeks indicated estimated fetal weight in the 94th percentile and normal placental vascular resistance.

A: Chronic abdominal aortopathy is suspected, potentially due to congenital abdominal aortic coarctation, fibromuscular dysplasia, or an inactive form of Takayasu's arteritis, based on well-developed collateral vasculature and lack of signs of active inflammation or neurofibromatosis/tuberculosis exposure.

P: Continue monitoring pregnancy and headaches. Patient instructed to continue current medications and attend regular check-ups. Advised to seek immediate contact if symptoms change or concerns arise.

S: Patient reports difficulty walking starting three days ago with discomfort in the front of the knee that progressed to pain. Denies prior injury or specific event. Reports no swelling. Previously received an intra-articular injection of xylocaine which provided temporary relief, followed by a catching sensation upon movement.
O: Physical examination tests (Lachman test, pivot-shift test, varus/valgus instability, McMurray test) were negative. Simple radiographs showed no abnormal findings. MRI revealed a soft tissue mass near the knee joint with an ill-defined border and high signal intensities on T1- and T2-weighted images; low signal intensity on fat-suppressed images; no contrast enhancement. Blood examination was normal. During surgery, a large fat mass with mobility was found on the anterior surface of the proximal-lateral PF joint and was removed via resection. Histology revealed connective tissue and fatty tissue without signs of lipoma, lipoma arborescens, or pigmented villonodular synovitis.
A: Soft tissue mass near the knee joint (anterior surface of the proximal-lateral PF joint) successfully removed via arthroscopy.
P: Knee arthroscopy performed to visualize and remove a soft tissue mass. Mass was found to be composed of fat with an ill-defined border. Symptoms have improved post-surgery, with no remaining signs of anterior knee pain or other issues. Follow-up recommended if symptoms return.

S: Patient reports right upper abdominal pain that has been quite bothersome.
O: CT scan without contrast media revealed a gallstone in the thickened gallbladder wall with a slight increase in CT value due to surrounding panniculitis. MRCP showed the cystic duct is connected to an aberrant bile duct. Intraoperative cholangiography revealed the aberrant right hepatic duct (ARHD) was not confluent with the major right branch of the intrahepatic bile duct and drained a narrow area.
A: Chronic calculous cholecystitis with aberrant bile duct flow into the cystic duct.
P: Laparoscopic cholecystectomy performed. ARHD was removed and ligated on both the hepatic side and the cystic duct using AESCULAP DS Titanium Lig. Post-operative follow-up recommended to monitor progress and ensure proper healing.

S: Patient reports a three-week history of intractable headache, confusion, vertical binocular diplopia, photophobia, and difficulty with balance.
O: Best corrected visual acuity was 20/25 in the right eye and 20/20 in the left eye. Intraocular pressures were 14 mmHg in both eyes. Anterior segment examination was unremarkable bilaterally. Funduscopic examination revealed grade-four optic disc edema, blurring of the optic disc margin, and obscuration of vasculature of the optic nerve in both eyes. Preretinal and intraretinal hemorrhages were present in both eyes. OCT confirmed optic nerve swelling on the retinal nerve fiber layer. Fluorescein angiography showed hyperfluorescence of the optic disc in both eyes. CT head, MRI brain, and MRV brain were unremarkable for intracranial mass, hemorrhage, or ischemia. CSF analysis revealed an opening pressure of 30 cm H2O, 77 WBC/mm3 with 94% lymphocytes, 93 mg/dL protein, and 73 mg/dL glucose. Bacterial and fungal cultures of the CSF were negative. CSF studies for Lyme, syphilis, herpes simplex virus, West Nile virus, enterovirus, syphilis, ANA, and p-ANCA were negative. Respiratory viral panel (adenovirus, CMV, influenza, parainfluenza, rhinovirus, RSV) was negative.
A: Preliminary assessment of optic nerve pathology with associated retinal hemorrhages and edema; no evidence of intracranial mass, hemorrhage, or ischemia identified on imaging.
P: Follow-up appointments and additional tests are needed to determine the cause of symptoms and develop a treatment plan.

S: Patient reports severe left back pain and left axillary numbness and paresthesia. Patient is a 53-year-old woman with posterior, stage IIB NSCLC in the left upper lobe who has received neoadjuvant carboplatin, pemetrexed, and radiotherapy.

O: Magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) studies showed no direct tumor invasion of the left brachial plexus or subclavian vessels.

A: Tumor attachment to the T2 and T3 vertebrae with infiltration of corresponding nerve roots is likely the cause of patient complaints.

P: Recommended treatment is a posterior approach, image-guided T2 and T3 osteotomy followed by transthoracic en bloc resection of the thoracic tumor. Patient provided informed consent for the procedure.

S: 70-year-old woman admitted for chest distress for 11 hours. Reports shortness of breath at rest and difficulty lying in the recumbent position. History of hypertension and diabetes mellitus, taking oral medication.
O: Heparin administered via arterial intrathecal injection (2000 units) and intravenous injection (3500 units). Prescribed medications included aspirin (100 mg/day), TiGraylo (90 mg every 12 h), and enoxaparin sodium (0.4 mL every 12 h subcutaneously) for 3 days. Laboratory results showed hemoglobin of 102 g/L, prothrombin time of 13.4 s, and international normalized ratio of 1.2. Physical examination revealed mild abdominal tenderness in the left lower quadrant, signs indicative of peritoneal irritation, and a neoplasm-like mucous clot connected to the bowel in the anus. Colonoscopy revealed a submucosal mass in the sigmoid colon with partially ruptured mucous membrane and clots causing obstruction. Abdominal CT scan showed a submucosal hematoma in the sigmoid colon; density of the mass did not significantly change on enhanced CT scan. The left flexure of the colon was thick.
A: Coronary atherosclerotic heart disease. Findings indicate issues with blood clotting. Submucosal mass and hematoma in the sigmoid colon.
P: Conservative treatment including stopping anticoagulant medications, providing total parenteral nutrition, and monitoring condition were attempted but did not resolve clinical symptoms. Plan to continue evaluation and discuss further treatment options.

S: Patient is a 64-year-old postmenopausal woman referred after a screening colonoscopy revealed adenocarcinoma. Patient reports being asymptomatic and denies palpable masses or lymphadenopathy prior to the colonoscopy. History includes hysterectomy secondary to symptomatic fibroids. Family history is negative for cancer.
O: Immunohistochemistry (IHC) of colonic lesion showed positive for CK-7, GATA-3, and ER; weakly positive for MOC-31; negative for CK-20, CD-X2, PR, PAX-8, SOX-10, CD45, chromogranin, synaptophysin, and TTF-1. CT of the chest, abdomen, and pelvis (August 2015) showed osteolytic thoracic vertebral and pelvic lesions, and bilateral axillary adenopathy measuring 1.4 cm on the right and 1.1 cm on the left. PET CT (October 2015) revealed metabolic activity in the right axilla and patchy radiotracer uptake involving the vertebral column corresponding to the CT findings. Fine needle aspiration (FNA) of the right axillary lymph node (November 2015) was negative for malignancy. CEA, CA 19-9, and CA-125 levels were within normal limits (CEA: 2.08 ng/mL, CA 19-9: <1 U/mL, CA-125: 6.4 U/mL). Bone biopsy of a right sacral lesion confirmed metastatic breast invasive ductal carcinoma with IHC positive for CK-7, GATA-3, ER, and PR but negative for CD45.
A: Metastatic breast invasive ductal carcinoma confirmed by bone biopsy; consistent with primary breast origin based on colonic lesion IHC findings. History of metastatic disease involving thoracic/pelvic lesions and bilateral axillary adenopathy.
P: Follow up with oncologist for close monitoring and further treatment options. Schedule regular appointments with the oncologist. Patient instructed to report any new symptoms or concerns during visits.

S: Patient reports pain and swelling in the right submandibular region for about 10 days. Symptoms are intermittent during meals but resolve after eating. Reports unpleasant sensations when eating sour or acidic food.
O: Extraoral swelling noted in the right submandibular region. Bimanual palpation revealed a firm swelling in the posterior floor of the mouth. A 7 mm spherical formation was identified.
A: Right submandibular salivary gland sialolithiasis (preliminary).
P: Computed tomography (CT) scan ordered to confirm diagnosis. If confirmed, surgical removal of the gland is planned, involving a Risdon incision, identification and protection of the marginal mandibular nerve, removal of the submandibular gland from the mylohyoid muscle, division and ligation of the submandibular duct, and removal of calculi. Postoperative plan includes placement of a suction drain and layered wound closure. Follow-up evaluations are essential to monitor recovery.

S: Patient reports difficulties with attention, restlessness, repetitive behaviors, and struggles with learning certain things. Patient also reports difficulty understanding things in logical areas such as math. Patient denies any other health problems.

O: Neuropsychological evaluation results from age 8.5 years old (WISC-III): VIQ = 88; PIQ = 117; TIQ = 102.

A: Preliminary assessment indicates difficulties in understanding, verbal fluency, and auditory attention based on historical neuropsychological evaluation results.

P: Patient advised to discuss the situation with parents and school to determine available support services. Recommended patient be patient and to work with a specialist.
